newsitem.title: INDIA: India asks army to help in truck strike.
newsitem.headline: India asks army to help in truck strike.

text.p: The Indian government asked the army on Thursday to help to move essential goods after more than two million striking truck owners kept their vehicles off the roads for a third day.
"The Defence Ministry has been advised to assist the state governments through the army where such services are required to ensure movement of essential commodities," a government spokesman said.
The strike has severely hit the movement of goods on roads and through ports and air cargo terminals and it could affect the entire economy, business leaders said.

The government spokesman said states had been asked to invoke the Essential Services Act, which empowers the government to declare the movement of goods an essential service and take punitive action against those blocking it.
"We have asked the states to intervene and make arrangements for movement of goods and services," Yogendra Narain, the highest ranking civil servant in the Surface Transport Ministry, told Reuters.
The truck owners, who launched the strike to protest against a proposed service tax and a rise in insurance premiums, scoffed at the government's move.

"They can try to suspend our permits or they can try to impound our vehicles, but from where will they get enough people to carry out these actions? There are three million of us," said All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC) spokesman S.P. Singh.
"It is a smokescreen to mislead people, an absolutely impractical suggestion," he said. "The strike will continue till our demands are met."
He estimated that the transport industry was suffering a loss of four billion rupees ($112 million) a day because of the strike.

The AIMTC represents owners of about two million heavy trucks, one million light and medium-weight trucks and about 60,000 booking and delivery companies. Truckers move about 60 percent of India's goods.

"Movement of export goods has already come to a halt. If the strike is allowed to continue, the entire economy will be paralysed," Ramu Deora, president of the Federation of Indian Exports Organisations, said in Bombay.
Industry and trade associations have urged the truck owners to call off the strike, which is pushing up prices of essential and perishable commodities.
"The ports have been affected. In Bombay, it has been fully affected," said Narain. On the eastern coast, the ports had been partially affected, he added.
Indian refineries had so far escaped largely unscathed but rising inventory levels could pose problems if the strike dragged on, oil industry officials said.
"It has not affected (oil industry) so far," a Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) official said.
But the supply of aviation fuel to airports could be hit if the strike continued for a few more days, industry sources said. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
